subject: HorizonTrust - Deployment attestation & attack lattice summary

Subject: HorizonTrust RFP - deployment isolation and attack surface details

Hi Stephanie,

Thanks for taking this on. HorizonTrust is running a focused security review for inference vendors as part of our Q2 procurement cycle. Attached is the formal RFP packet (HorizonTrust_Security_RFP_v2.pdf) — a few of our engineers called out the items below as highest priority for the initial submission: 

- A deployment topology: how customers are isolated (VPC/tenant model), traffic egress flows, and bastion/access patterns.
- Isolation controls: sidecar/proxy architecture, KV cache handling, and whether any persistent shared storage is used.
- Threat summary: likely attack lattice/paths for lateral movement and mitigations (brief).
- Evidence: sample artifact(s) that show the controls you reference (diagrams, config excerpts, SOC2 references).

Can you provide a concise attestation and the topology diagram by next Friday (5/6)? We may follow up with a deeper technical call focused on sidecar egress and KV cache behavior.

Also, please copy whoever owns security at Redwood — we'll need their technical point of contact if we have clarifying questions.

Thanks,
Alex

Alex — thanks for the packet and the clear priority list. Attaching our current topology diagram (rnw-inference-topology-v3.svg) and a short isolation attestation (isolation-attestation-summary.pdf) to this reply.

High-level answers up front:
- Multi-tenant isolation is provided by a combination of VPC tenancy + per-tenant logical partitioning in the serving layer; no tenant shares persistent disk.
- Sidecar proxies control all north-south and egress flows; default posture is deny-all outbound, with allowlists for destination services (metrics, KMS, model registry).
- KV cache lives in process/GPU memory per request session; we rotate and zero memory on session termination and do not persist KV to shared disk.

I'll loop Rishi (security owner) and Irene (infrastructure) to the thread for any deeper technical detail. Proposed next steps: quick architecture walk (30 mins) early next week — does Monday 5/3 or Tuesday 5/4 work for you? I can send a calendar invite.

Attachments: rnw-inference-topology-v3.svg, isolation-attestation-summary.pdf

Stephanie — appreciate the quick reply and the attachments. A few follow-ups from our security engineering team after a review:

1) Sidecar egress enforcement: can you confirm whether egress allowlists are enforced at the kernel/networking layer (iptables/ebpf) in the node, or entirely within the sidecar process? We need to understand the enforcement boundary and whether a compromise of the sidecar could bypass the policy.

2) KV cache lifecycle: your note about zeroing memory is helpful. Can you provide more specifics: is the cache ever paged to swap or ephemeral disk under memory pressure? Is the keying process per-request or per-tenant session?

3) Multi-tenant compute: you mention VPC + logical partitioning. Do you ever colocate customer compute on the same GPU host? If so, what are the guardrails (cgroups, process namespace isolation, hypervisor fence)?

4) Canary / failover: we require a clear rollout plan with automated rollback triggers for model and serving changes (percent rollout, error/latency thresholds). Can you sketch your canary plan and the rollback conditions you use in practice?

Finally, can you include any pertinent SOC2 section references or a short note about audit log retention (how long token-level logs are retained and how they are scoped to customers)?

We'd like those answers before the architecture call so our engineers can review.

Thanks,
Alex
From: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie.nguyen@redwood.com>
To: Alex Garner <alex.garner@horizontrust.com>
Cc: rishi_malhotra@redwood.com, irene_choi@redwood.com, procurement@horizontrust.com
Date: Fri, 30 Apr 2027 15:42:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: HorizonTrust RFP - deployment isolation and attack surface details

Alex — thanks, good questions. See concise answers below and attached evidence bundle (evidence-pack.zip) that includes kernel-level config excerpts, our SOC2 certification summary, and a sample audit-log extract.

1) Sidecar egress enforcement
- Enforcement layers: allowlists are implemented in three layers for defense-in-depth: 
  a. Sidecar process enforces application-level allowlists and TLS routing (primary control).
  b. Node-level eBPF/XDP program enforces a hard network policy (deny-by-default) that only permits approved CIDRs/ports; this is kernel-enforced and survives a sidecar process compromise.
  c. Cloud VPC SG/ACL controls provide an additional coarse filter at the subnet edge.
- Implication: a compromised sidecar cannot create arbitrary outbound connections; it would need kernel-level exploit to evade eBPF policy. See evidence-pack.zip:/ebpf-policy-excerpt.txt.

2) KV cache lifecycle and memory handling
- Storage: KV cache is in-GPU and in-process CPU memory only. We do not write KV cache to persistent disk.
- Memory pressure: we never swap KV cache to disk; OS swap is disabled on ded-tenant runtime hosts and memory pressure triggers eviction policies (LRU) within the process. Evicted fragments are zeroed before reuse.
- Keying: KV keys are scoped per-session and tagged with tenant id; caches are garbage-collected on session close and on tenant shutdown.

3) Multi-tenant compute and colocation
- Colocation model: in our hosted offering customers may share GPU hosts subject to tenant isolation gates; dedicated and private deployments provide non-colocated options.
- Guardrails for shared hosts: process namespace isolation (Linux namespaces), strict cgroup limits, Seccomp filters, and mandatory eBPF network policy. Additionally, we use inference runtime sandboxes that ensure memory isolation between model workers.
- We include documented attestations when we colocate: workload placement policies and evidence (included in evidence-pack.zip:/colocation-guardrails.md).

4) Canary/Failover plan
- Rollout steps: canary deploy -> progressive ramp (1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 100%) with automated monitors.
- Triggers for automatic rollback: token error rate > 1.5x baseline OR median token latency > 2x baseline OR regression on quality checks for a sentinel prompt set. Rollbacks are automated by the platform orchestration layer and alert owners immediately.

5) SOC2 / Audit logs
- SOC2: Redwood is SOC2 Type II certified (certificate excerpt in evidence pack).
- Audit logs: request- and token-level logs retained by default for 90 days for hosted customers; extended retention available as an enterprise add-on. Logs are partitioned by account id and accessible via the Console or secure S3 export; KMS-wrapped at rest.

Next steps:

- If helpful, Rishi can join the call and walk through the eBPF policy and evidence artifacts.
